title_en: Meta launches Muse in UK – the AI agent that can do your Christmas shopping
excerpt_en: Users can give agents tasks such as booking travel or buying presents but glitches have been reported
body_en: Want to avoid the Christmas shopping hordes? Then let your AI agent do it. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on their apps – and the high street.
Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

Muse can be used as an app or directly within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. Meta invites users to give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, so they can talk to it as well as assign it tasks such as sending an email, booking travel or buying festive presents.
“From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you,” said Meta.

Meta acknowledged that handing control of your day-to-day digital life to an AI agent is “an act of trust”. Muse cannot make a purchase or send an email without your permission and will only connect to apps you let it join. The app has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods, Meta said, and it does not share your conversations with advertisers. It will ask for your approval before making a purchase or sending an email, while a separate “security agent” checks Muse’s actions against the permissions you’ve granted.

“Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar,” said Meta. “To get those jobs done, you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.”

Meta said it has signed deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, electrical retailer Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily.

In a statement last month UK regulators including the Competition and Markets Authority and the Information Commissioner’s Office said AI agents – the term for AI programmes that carry out series of tasks without human intervention – could “unlock wider innovation” but could also “amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones”. The watchdogs said concerns such as fraud, scams and misuse of personal information needed to be addressed by companies providing personal AI agents.

Reuters reported last week that Meta employees had raised concerns about the app’s performance, including one staff member receiving a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an encrypted messaging app. In another example reported by Reuters, Muse delivered a message with random bank account balances in it.

Meta said internal testing is vital for product development and allows the company to implement safety and privacy protection before releasing anything publicly. It is understood the majority of problems flagged by Reuters related to a bug that has been fixed.

Muse is powered by Muse Spark, Meta’s first model from the company’s “super intelligence” AI lab. In a social media post on Sunday, Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, raised the possibility of humanity losing control over AI systems that are able to improve themselves autonomously.
“It is … hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with super intelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field,” he wrote.

Responding to reports that AI had cracked one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – the Riemann hypothesis – Wang said the tech industry needed to make progress in the “extremely urgent” areas of AI safety, security and alignment. Alignment refers to ensuring an AI system adheres to human goals and values.

title_en: Country diary: A close watch on this autumn’s leaf fall – it’s been unpredictable | Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
excerpt_en: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe
body_en: Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground.

There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. Instead, it holds them close – a burnished bronze, brighter even than its neighbour’s gold. To the left, a greener tree stands on the end of the line.
Related: Country diary: The autumn glory of a tulip tree | Jennifer Jones

The changing colours of the leaves of deciduous trees, and the timing of their fall, has been particularly unpredictable this year. Many trees here in the south-west have experienced stress during the hot summer and drought, with some shedding leaves early in response and others displaying more muted autumn colours, or adjusting the timing of their changes in shade.

In the extreme heat driven by the climate crisis, ecosystems are increasingly pushed into “ false autumn ” cycles. Trees with shallower root systems can struggle to reach deeper moisture reserves, dropping their leaves early to conserve water and energy. These oaks, with their deeper roots, may have fared better with increased access to water.

This year, I have been watching the shedding of the leaves of my nearest trees more keenly. I have seen the occasional leaf drop from the silver birch by the house – a shallower rooted tree that, unlike many others of its kind, did not let its leaves go prematurely, though it has foregone its usual vibrancy. The neighbouring beeches, lining a field in the valley, lost theirs early yet some still hold patches of buttery colour. Now, this oak’s are the latest to go, dropped with conviction, while the flanking trees stand unmoved. Amid the uncertainty, it seems to know just when to let go and with what vigour to release its gold.
• Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title_en: Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
excerpt_en: Awareness campaign reminds public ‘traffic is a team sport’ amid less civility and more collisions on roads
body_en: For decades the Netherlands has been famed for its proud cycling culture, with a network of 23,000 miles of bike paths used by everyone from children under eight to adults over 80.

In recent years, however, like so many countries around the world, it has seen a dramatic change in the type of vehicles using those lanes: no longer the preserve of pedal bikes, they are used by all manner of two-wheeled vehicles including electric cargo bikes, thick-tyred “fatbikes”, speed pedelecs, electric scooters and even some micro cars.

Throw smartphones into the mix as well, say critics, and the result is clear: less space, more conflict, less civility and more collisions. According to the Netherlands Institute for Transport Policy Analysis, the annual number of cyclist deaths increased by more than 50% between 2015 and 2025.
What is needed, say some, are new rules of the road (or, at least, path). Last week, the Dutch government sent a bill to parliament proposing mandatory helmets for under-18s on ebikes.

The moves are welcomed by those who feel that things need to change. As one resident, Patrick van den Hoven, wrote in the Amsterdam newspaper Het Parool this month: “Let’s call a spade a spade: [ebikes] are vehicles with a motor, which, as far as I am concerned, we should treat as motor vehicles.”
The city’s bike lanes now resembled “a permanent traffic experiment”, he said, adding: “The bicycle made our country great. It would be a shame if it eventually fell victim to electric progress.”

Another city, Leiden, launched a public awareness campaign earlier this month to remind everyone that “traffic is a team sport”. It has the Netherlands’ highest number bike accidents per head, and cyclist injuries have risen by more than half since 2018.

“This campaign aims to say: guys, watch out for one another,” said Julius Terpstra, the deputy mayor for spatial planning and mobility. “We see more people on bikes, more older people on bikes due to the ageing population, and more different vehicles, when once the Netherlands only had the Gazelle [a famed brand of pedal bike]. We see national trends here too: the rise of the electric bike, more telephone use, and also drug use.”

According to Florrie de Pater, a board member of the Fietsersbond Amsterdam cycling union, there has been a notable decline in road manners. “There is less consideration for one another and less empathy among cyclists, perhaps also because we live in an individualistic world where everything has to go fast, fast, fast,” she said.

Romee Nicolai, the bicycle mayor of Amsterdam, believes some people have forgotten that the extensive network of dedicated cycle paths was created after a wave of activism sparked by road deaths in the 1970s.

“People have been cycling for hundreds of years, but we need to acknowledge that this cannot continue if we don’t give it attention,” she said. “You can’t grow plants if you don’t give them attention and water, and it’s the same with cycling. That means public debate, and financial means from government to create a safe cycling environment too.”

Some older people have told her they are too afraid of an accident to get on their bicycles, while one in five children are growing up without a cycling culture. “We need to acknowledge that we are actually losing those cyclists,” Nicolai said.

The National Institute for Public Health and the Environment found in a recent study that fewer Dutch young adults were doing the recommended daily amount of movement, partly owing to less general cycling and the rise of the electric bike.

Jasper Reenalda, a human movement scientist at the University of Twente, has some concerns about the impact of more ebike use, particularly if children lose a low-impact exercise that was once built into everyday life.

“Our whole infrastructure was built around bikes, so children bike to school, they bike to sports, they bike to all kinds of social activities,” he said. “It was always very easy for Dutch children to reach the norms of active, minimally active behaviour. If children are switching to ebikes, and that’s the trend, it is more challenging to reach the minimum number of active minutes to stay healthy.”

However, some experts warn it is easy to stereotype certain groups – such as “ fatbike” users – for causing the tensions. Clara Glachant, a researcher in micromobility at Eindhoven University of Technology, said electric bikes could have a positive role in “expanding cycling to groups that do not cycle”.

Meredith Glaser, the chief executive of the Urban Cycling Institute in Amsterdam, said four in 10 cyclists who died in recent years were in a collision with a car. “Any pointing of fingers towards cyclists is an excellent scapegoat for the uncomfortable reality that cars and trucks are still taking up the majority of public space and causing the most harm to the environment and to human bodies,” she said.

title_en: PNG’s parliament is voting on ratifying Bougainville independence. A ‘no’ won’t be the end of the story
excerpt_en: After more than a century of colonial rule, a brutal war and a hard-won peace, Bougainville is approaching the finals steps of its road to self-determination.
body_en: In a 2019 referendum, close to 98% of Bougainvilleans for independence. After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process.
In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result.
A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving.

Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track.

The legacy of colonialism Bougainville was named by French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville in the 18th century, and colonialism has shaped its history ever since. In 1899, it was incorporated into German New Guinea, while the neighbouring Solomon Islands became a British protectorate.

Colonial control shifted to Australian occupation in 1914, a move legitimised by the League of Nations in 1920. During the second world war, Japanese forces took over, followed by an American-led invasion in 1943.

From 1949, Bougainville was again under Australian control as part of PNG. The dismantling of colonial rule began in 1971, and PNG gained independence in 1975. Bougainville’s decolonisation was left unresolved.
The crisis years From 1988 to 1998, Bougainville experienced one of the most severe conflicts in the South Pacific.

The Panguna mine was a focal point for grievances related to land ownership, environmental damage, a desire for self-determination and the distribution of mining resources. The mine began operating in 1972 in Central Bougainville, and was once one of the world’s one of the world’s largest copper and gold mines. Owned by a subsidiary of the Australian company Rio Tinto, it was a significant source of revenue for the PNG government.
In the late 1980s, the environmental impacts of mining and unequal distribution of its revenues led to violent protests by landowners and the closure of the mine.

The PNG government responded with force, and the protests developed into an armed rebellion. Conflict ensued, involving the Bougainville Revolutionary Army, the PNG Defence Force and various local factions. Australia provided indirect military support to PNG forces.
A years-long PNG-imposed blockade paralysed Bougainville’s government services and economic activity. An estimated 15,000–20,000 lives were lost in the conflict overall.

Attempts to end the fighting began with people from local villages, especially women. They used customary and introduced conflict resolution processes, alongside Christian faith, to lay the groundwork for political negotiations.
Eventually, peace talks began in 1998, and an agreement was signed in 2001.
Two narratives about how peace was achieved There have long been two narratives about Bougainville’s path to peace.
One emphasises regional and international diplomacy, which has involved New Zealand‑facilitated talks in 1997–98, unarmed Australian peace monitoring and UN engagement.
The second, backed by many Bougainvillean and PNG leaders, stresses a “ light intervention ” of international support and notes the distinctly Melanesian approach to peacemaking.
This process has been inclusive (involving women’s groups, young people, ex-combatants, faith-based organisations and churches) and patient.

The Bougainville Peace Agreement In 2001, the Bougainville Peace Agreement established a framework for Bougainville’s political future. The agreement led to the establishment of the autonomous Bougainville government, a weapons-disposal program, free and fair elections, and a referendum on Bougainville’s future political status.

The 2019 referendum gave Bougainvilleans a decisive mandate. Then in August of this year, the autonomous Bougainville government and PNG government – with international support – set out a jointly agreed, phased pathway to translate the referendum result into a constitutional transition.
Now, the results must be ratified by PNG’s parliament – the final legislative step in the peace agreement process.
A “yes” vote will not itself create independence. It will kick off the legal, administrative and institutional actions needed to move towards self‑government and ultimately independence.

title_en: A slash-and-burn budget update could push Australia into a recession. Jim Chalmers has a fine line to tread | Patrick Commins
excerpt_en: Labor has been complacent. But deep cuts designed to kill inflation would come at least six months too late
body_en: A pivot towards austerity in next month’s mid-year budget would come far too late in the battle against inflation and risk pushing Australia into a recession we don’t need to have.
This is a truth that Jim Chalmers came halfway to articulating in Monday’s special economic statement, delivered during question time.
The treasurer revealed that unemployment is forecast to rise above 5% by the middle of next year. Inflation is expected to remain higher than wanted, at about 3.5%.
Growth is predicted to slow to “well below” 2% and stay there for a couple of years – much less than the usually expected growth rate of at least 2.75%.

Listening to the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, you would think the best plan of attack would be deep budget cuts designed to kill inflation once and for all. He continues to argue that every dollar of government spending is “debt petrol poured in the inflation fire”.
But that is a solution that would be at least six months too late.
Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, goes further. She reckons blaming government spending for today’s inflation problem “is about two years too late”.

Wilson is not explicitly calling for a slash-and-burn budget. He knows that would be political cyanide. But he’s happy to create the impression that this is what is needed and in so doing has created an impossible test for the government’s fiscal management.
Labor could have perhaps made a difference in the May budget but instead announced policies that added $11.8bn to net spending through 2025-26 and 2026-27.
Wilson is on firmer ground when he criticises this, arguing: “We warned about the risk of inflation and they spent anyway.”

This is the half of the truth that Chalmers is less willing to acknowledge. The government did indeed keep announcing new spending measures while inflation was climbing rapidly through the second half of 2025 and into 2026.
It was complacent about the inflation challenge. But that was then and this is now. The balance of risks has shifted from worrying about high inflation and towards fretting about rising unemployment.

The Reserve Bank’s top officials may not be quite there but at least three of its board members showed they had already accepted this reality when they voted against the latest rate hike. Their position looked much stronger when the jobless rate last week jumped to 4.9%.
Private sector economists are even more pessimistic than the forecasts outlined by Chalmers on Monday. Some predict the jobless rate will reach 5.5% in a year’s time.
AMP’s Shane Oliver reckons economic growth could fall below 1% and Australia will “flirt with a recession” in 2027.
Does this sound like an economy in need of a slash-and-burn budget?

Again, listening to the opposition, you might think the answer is still a yes. Chalmers knows this argument has established deep roots in the community, with many people now blaming public spending for driving rising inflation.
It means the treasurer will try to strike what he calls a “delicate balance” in the budget update – what he describes as “cutting spending enough, without threatening growth”.
“At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions without slashing and burning the services people rely on,” he told parliament.
It’s not at all clear that the electorate will accept this nuanced message.
But the government will hope it will be enough to get to the other side of Christmas without losing any more votes on economic management.
• Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

title_en: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
excerpt_en: The post Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A commuter riding the Metro in Washington, D.C., snapped photos of a man working on a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” Obtained by ProPublica Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.
Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.
Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica? If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

Send Us a Tip The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

title_en: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
excerpt_en: The post If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported? appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A tres leches cake is cut and served during a support group in Kent County, Michigan, for immigrant women who have experienced domestic abuse. Jamie Kelter Davis for ProPublica About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.

I’m a ProPublica reporter in Detroit, and my colleague Melissa Sanchez is in Chicago. We each drove over 100 miles last summer to be in this room because we were working on a story. It published in mid-October, and it’s about how the immigration policies of President Donald Trump’s administration have made life more perilous for victims of domestic abuse. While reporting, we had heard about the pervasive presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in west Michigan, and we wanted to hear from immigrant women there who were living through domestic abuse. How did they weigh whether it was safer to stay with an abusive partner or to seek help from law enforcement, knowing they might be detained — and even deported?

That night, a young woman with a toddler told us that she called 911 about a year earlier, after her boyfriend slapped her when he was drunk. If he hit her today, she said, she wouldn’t dial that number again. With arrests by federal immigration officers constantly in the news, she said, the risk is too great.

None of the others in the room said they were currently living with an abusive partner. Those women were out there, the group’s facilitators told us. But they were too afraid to even leave their homes.

Children play while their relatives take part in the support group. Jamie Kelter Davis for ProPublica After the meeting, as empty paper plates were cleared from the tables, the facilitators told us about E. She was once a regular at the meetings, they said, but hadn’t been around in a while. They worried about her. We asked if E. might be open to talking with us and, after a few texts, we learned that she was — if we could be ready to talk in about 20 minutes.

We hurried back to our nearby lodgings, dialed E.’s number and put her on speakerphone. In Spanish, Melissa explained what we were reporting on, why it was so important to hear from somebody like her and the kinds of questions we wanted to ask. Then we began the interview.

E., who asked not to be fully identified, told us that she avoids going out unless it’s absolutely necessary. She’d heard harrowing stories about women at the immigration detention center in Michigan where other women we’d interviewed were locked up. As we described in our story, several had been arrested here in Kent County when local police responded to domestic violence calls. E. doesn’t want to end up in ICE custody herself or, worse, deported.
For the sake of her kids, E. said, she tolerates her husband’s abuse in silence.

When he tells her she’s “nobody here” and to “go back to your country,” she said she puts her head down. When he pulls her hair in bed and says she belongs to him, she said she pretends it’s a joke. When he asks for the money she makes from selling food at a local factory, she said she hands it over.

A filing in E.’s immigration case says her husband is a U.S. citizen who has been “verbally and financially abusive” and has threatened to take away the child they share. E. said that, except for the hair pulling, he isn’t physically abusive.
For help in English or Spanish, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788.

(Like the other women we interviewed, E. asked that ProPublica not interview her alleged abuser because she’s afraid he will retaliate against her, take away her children or call ICE. To report these women’s stories, we interviewed attorneys, advocates, family and others who interacted with them. When available, we also reviewed text messages, and records from law enforcement and immigration court.)

E. said her husband doesn’t overtly threaten her with calling ICE. But she said she found a hotline number for the agency written in his journal, alongside a description of his ideal woman: obedient and submissive.

That reminded us of what a local immigration attorney, Catherine Villanueva, had told us: “We have this idea that we’re deporting these really bad people,” she said. “What we’re doing is we’re empowering the bad people who are already here.”

We asked E. if she had ever called the police to report her husband’s abuse. Her answer came quickly: No. Her husband is frail. She worries police officers will look at both of them and decide that he’s the victim. “They won’t see me as the abused one,” she said. “If I called the police, the one who would wind up losing is me.”

title_en: Did you solve it? How Super Mario explains Renaissance art
body_en: Earlier today I set you the following puzzle. Here it is again with the solution.
Consider a simplified game of Super Mario. He moves from platform to platform. He can either step forward 1 space, to the next platform, or jump forward 2 spaces, to the platform after that.
He starts on the first platform. How many ways are there for Mario to land on the last platform if the level has:
And what has this got to do with Leonardo da Vinci?
We begin by listing the possible routes across each level.
3 platforms: to cross from the first to the third there are two routes:
4 platforms: to cross from the first to the fourth there are three routes:
5 platforms: to cross from the first to the fifth there are five routes:
That’s enough enumeration. There’s a quicker way to do this. Notice that the number of routes on a level with n platforms is simply the sum of the totals of levels with n – 1 and n – 2 platforms.

For example, with 6 platforms, illustrated above, there are two choices for the first move – a step or a jump - to either A or B. From A the problem has reduced to a level with 5 platforms (five routes), and from B to four platforms (three routes). So the total is five + three = eight routes.
So with 7 platforms, there are thirteen routes (8 + 5).
With 8 platforms there are twenty-one (13 + 8).

The sequence in bold may be familar to some readers. It is the Fibonacci sequence, named after the Italian mathematician who wrote about it in the early 13th century. It starts with 0, 1, and every new term is the sum of the two previous terms.
Fibonacci was also known as Leonardo da Pisa, but the question asked about his namesake Leonardo da Vinci. The Fibonacci sequence links to the painter of the Mona Lisa via the golden ratio.
Consider ratio of consecutive terms of the Fibonaci sequence from 1:

These terms converge on a number, the golden ratio, which is 1.618 to three decimal places. The golden ratio can also be constructed geometrically: imagine a rectangle with long side A and short side B. If (A+B)/A = A/B, then A/B = 1.618…
In 1509, Luca Pacioli published a book about the golden ratio that was illustrated by Leonardo da Vinci. It was called Divina Proportione, divine proportion.

The book helped popularise the idea that the golden ratio captures beauty. While there is no scientific proof that that humans are more attracted to the golden ratio than to any other ratio, many artists, architects and plastic surgeons use the golden ratio in their work.

Thanks to Dr Tom Crawford for today’s puzzle. His new book How Many Pikachus Would it Take to Power a Lightbulb? asks entertaining questions about fantasy worlds and answers them with proper maths. The books is available at the Guardian Bookshop.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

title_en: ‘Most of the video budget went on Steve Strange’s makeup’: Midge Ure on how Visage made Fade to Grey
excerpt_en: ‘I was really into pre-Raphaelite paintings – Millais’ drowning Ophelia and the like – so I wrote a romantic study that eventually became this’
body_en: Midge Ure, singer, songwriter Visage were an amalgamation of three bands: Rich Kids, Magazine and Ultravox. Since all three were touring, getting everybody in the studio at the same time was nigh on impossible. Still, we were making our debut album and were a track short, when along came this gift from God.

We had no money so I’d been moonlighting with Thin Lizzy, and keyboardist Billy Currie had been playing with Gary Numan. Fade to Grey started life as an instrumental that Billy had been jamming with Chris Payne from the Numan band in soundchecks. They’d tried to release it but nobody was interested. I thought it was wonderful and suggested writing lyrics so we could use it on the Visage album.
The song and the video just seemed to capture a moment: the Blitz club, New Romantics, synthesisers

The instrumental created this brilliant atmosphere – mysterious, melancholy, dark, dystopian, film noir – which put pictures in my head. I imagined a guy sitting on a train station with a suitcase, trying to escape his life, hence: “One man on a lonely platform, one case sitting by his side …” There’s a term in video-making, “fade to black”, but I changed it for the song because it gave the impression of a transition to something else. I imagined the man getting on a train not knowing where he’d end up.

The music was already recorded so we didn’t do a huge amount to it. I think Rusty Egan played some electronic drums. Steve Strange was the frontman but wasn’t a natural singer. So I put down a vocal, then he sang while listening to my vocal in headphones – what came out of his mouth was the same melody, but in his voice. You can hear me on the “aahs”, the “fade to greys” and some of the harmony parts. Rusty had a Belgian girlfriend, Brigitte Arendt, so someone – probably Rusty – suggested she read the title in French along with a translation of the lyrics. It was the icing on the cake.

Godley and Creme wanted to showcase themselves as video-makers so they made one for us for just £1,500: most of that went on makeup artists for Steve. The song and the video just seemed to capture a moment: the Blitz club, New Romantics, synthesisers. Then suddenly it was in the charts all over Europe.

Chris Payne, keyboards, songwriter Fade to Grey started off in 1976 or 77 when I was a music student at Chichester and we had to compose something. I was really into pre-Raphaelite paintings – Millais’ Ophelia and the like – so I wrote a romantic study with the chords that eventually became Fade to Grey, but played on piano in a different manner. After I joined the Gary Numan band, I used to mess around playing the chords on a Polymoog synth and a bassline on a Minimoog. One day Billy and drummer Cedric Sharpley joined in. As the tour progressed, we developed it in soundchecks.

After the tour, Billy was due to go back to Ultravox, so we wanted to record it as a keepsake. We used producer Martin Rushent’s studio in London, but when we set up the gear the Minimoog wasn’t there, just the Polymoog. However, the brass setting gave the bassline the distinctive attack on Fade to Grey. Cedric started the song with a CR-78 drum machine and put the drums down. Billy sprinkled synth over it and that was it. The arrangement was created on the fly. Then Billy called asking: “Do you mind if it goes on the Visage album?”
Related: Steve Strange: a beautiful maverick who understood the power of myth

And the rest is history. The next thing I knew my publisher called me to say it was at No 45. Then my neighbour came in going: “It’s on Top of the Pops! And there’s this most amazing video.” Then it was in the Top 10 – and No 1 in some countries.
I’m really happy with its success. On YouTube, there are loads of people doing different takes. I’ve just done a version for Midge’s new album, and my wife sang the French bit. It’s come full circle.

• Midge Ure’s Chapters: The Best Of is out now on CD, 2LP and a 3CD deluxe version including Chris Payne’s remix. A new version of Fade to Grey is available digitally and on 7” vinyl from midgeure.tmstor.es. Midge Ure is on tour this month

title_en: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
excerpt_en: Division over fossil fuels at this year’s UN climate summit scotched any hope of a deal – despite Australian efforts.
body_en: Chris McGrath/Getty Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.
Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations and Australia’s Minister for Climate Change, speaks to the media after the final session during the second overtime day of the climate talks. Chris McGrath/Getty

No mention of the ‘F’ word For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “ transition away from fossil fuels ”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.
The Dubai text was hailed as “ the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era ”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.
Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”.
This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “ 35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

Activist Greta Thunberg attends a protest at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Burak Kara/Getty The “COP of action” fails to deliver This year’s climate summit was billed as an “ implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as “ president of negotiations ”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

title_en: Why fossil fuel-producing countries are stalling this crucial climate report
excerpt_en: Independent, expert climate science is critical to our future.
body_en: Muhammad Fajri/Getty After a year of record-breaking weather and a “super” El Niño underway, there’s no doubt climate extremes are wreaking havoc across the globe.

For decades, scientists have warned us this would happen. Their research made the case for reducing fossil fuel dependence. And we’ve relied on their expertise to assess the severity and extent of climate change.

But a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries is now obstructing the publication of a key scientific report from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This threatens global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. And it has created deep concern at the COP31 climate summit, currently in its final hours in Turkey, also known as Türkiye.

A truly global report First, it helps to understand why this report is so significant. The IPCC is the UN body for assessing the science related to climate change. Established in 1988, it provides political leaders with independent scientific assessments on climate change and strategies for response.

This panel has produced six pivotal reports to date, which have collated and reviewed the latest knowledge on climate change science. And over the past two years, more than 640 experts from around the world have been meeting to write the seventh.

The authors are leading researchers who volunteer their time. More than half of the authors working on the current seventh report, called the Seventh Assessment Report, or AR7, are from developing countries. I am a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports in the working group that looks at impacts, vulnerability and adaptation.
Work on this seventh report kicked off in December 2024, and its timeline for completion was never officially finalised.
What’s the hold-up? Originally, the plan was for the seventh report to be released in 2028. But five countries are objecting to this timeline and pushing for a later release in 2029.
India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya and China are ostensibly arguing that countries from the global south lack the resources and capacity to meet the current deadline.
However, these countries also happen to be among the world’s largest fossil fuel producers.

If recent reports are anything to go by, the evidence of global warming in this seventh report is likely to be alarming. It will highlight the evidence for much greater action, including deep and urgent reduction in fossil fuel production and use.

Extending the release date means IPCC contributors would have even more information they would have to assess. This delay would increase, not alleviate, the demands of authorship and reviewing for those contributors from developing nations.

The disagreement resulted in the suspension of the latest IPCC meeting in October in Ethiopia, with no confirmed timeline for the report release or budget for 2027. This threatens the very existence of the IPCC.

Nations seeking delay argue that tight timelines are unfair to developing countries. But the least developed countries (LDC), a group comprised of 44 nations, expressed “ deep disappointment ” when the meeting in Ethiopia was suspended.
Why the deadline matters Every five years, the UN’s climate body does a global stocktake of how effectively the world is responding to climate change.

Intended to ramp up climate action, these stocktakes take a long hard look at the state of the planet, identify the gaps in our approach and suggest a path forward. To be truly effective, these must be based on the latest science.

Delaying the seventh report would mean the most recent science is not fed into the 2028 global stocktake. This has grave implications for future climate action, and any delay in our response could have catastrophic effects on the wellbeing of planetary and human health.
Science vs politics While major fossil-fuel-emitting countries often attempt to impede phaseout efforts, undermining the IPCC follows a recent trend of discrediting science for political ends.

After a UN report in September found that limiting global warming to 1.5°C was no longer possible, Saudi Arabia jumped to question the credibility of the science, contending the research was not peer-reviewed. In fact, the report had been written over the course of a year by 44 experts, and reviewed by a further 44.

Conflict at COP31 Despite opposition to delaying the IPCC report, those pushing for it have remained unmoved at COP31. Speaking to media at the summit, former US Vice President Al Gore accused Saudi Arabia of trying to sabotage the IPCC’s work.
“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” he said.
